body:
What is a geographical indication?

A geographical indication (GI) identifies goods as originating in a particular country, region or locality when a specific quality, reputation or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. In simple terms, a GI connects the identity of a product with the place from which it comes.

Gujarat provides many examples. Patan Patola is associated with a particular weaving tradition, Gir Kesar Mango with a recognised agricultural product, and Kutch Ajrakh with a regional textile-printing tradition. In each case, the geographical name has significance because of the recognised characteristics or reputation of the goods.

Geographical indication: An indication identifying goods whose quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially linked to their geographical origin.

What creates the geographical connection?

The connection may arise from natural conditions, inherited human skills, or a combination of both.

  • Natural factors: Soil, climate, local growing conditions or naturally occurring materials may influence the characteristics of agricultural or natural products.
  • Human factors: Traditional techniques, specialised craftsmanship and knowledge developed by a community may give manufactured goods a distinctive identity.
  • Reputation: Buyers may recognise a product by its established association with a place, even when every distinguishing feature cannot be reduced to one physical measurement.

The legal test is not that every product from a place automatically deserves a GI. There must be a demonstrable connection between the identified goods, the defined geographical area and the relevant quality, reputation or characteristic.

Which goods can receive GI protection?

India's GI law covers agricultural goods, natural goods and manufactured goods. Handicrafts and food products can fall within the applicable categories. For manufactured goods, at least one of the activities of production, processing or preparation must take place in the defined geographical territory.

This requirement explains why a traditional craft can qualify. Its identity may depend on a technique preserved by artisans in a particular area, rather than on the chemical composition of its raw materials alone.

A GI is linked to goods, not to services. A geographical name used merely as an attractive business name is not automatically a GI. Indications determined to be generic names for goods cannot be registered as GIs.

Why GIs matter to Gujarat's economy

Traditional crafts and specialised agricultural products often involve small producers. These producers may face competition from cheaper imitations, limited access to distant markets and weak recognition of their work. A GI provides a legal basis for distinguishing authentic origin-linked goods from misleadingly labelled products.

Economic benefits are possible when protection is combined with effective marketing, consistent product characteristics, producer organisation and consumer awareness. Better recognition may support sales, rural employment and the continuation of traditional skills. However, GI registration does not automatically guarantee higher prices, exports or increased income.

There is also an important connection with innovation. Craftspersons may improve designs, packaging and production practices while preserving the features that define their GI product. Such improvements can increase commercial value without changing the geographical identity of the underlying goods.

India's legal framework

The principal law is the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. Its provisions came into force on 15 September 2003. The Geographical Indications Registry has its head office at Chennai and exercises jurisdiction throughout India.

The year in the Act's title and the year it came into force are different. This distinction is useful when remembering the development of India's GI protection system.

Prelims focus

  • A GI identifies goods through their geographical origin and an associated quality, reputation or other characteristic.
  • India's GI law is the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999.
  • The Act came into force on 15 September 2003.
  • The GI Registry's head office is in Chennai.
  • GIs can cover agricultural, natural and manufactured goods, including qualifying handicrafts.
  • Trap: A product does not qualify merely because its name contains a place name.

[Sources: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 2(1)(e), 5, 8 and 9; Government of India, Gazette Notifications S.O. 1051(E) and S.O. 1052(E), 15 September 2003; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, chapter 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, chapter 6, 'Rural Development', printed pp. 100–101; legal and online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Geographical Indications: How Place Creates Product Identity

body:
Who can apply to register a GI?

A GI normally represents the interests of a group of producers rather than one business seeking ownership of an ordinary brand name. Under India's GI Act, an association of persons or producers, an organisation, or an authority established by or under law may apply when it represents the interests of the producers of the relevant goods.

An application must identify the goods and the geographical territory concerned. It must also explain the connection between the goods and their origin, including relevant characteristics, methods of production and arrangements for maintaining the required standards.

The applicant's place of business is not necessarily the geographical area covered by the GI. For example, a body based in a city may represent producers located in a different, specifically defined production region.

How registration takes place

The main stages are application, examination, publication, opportunity for opposition and registration. An accepted application is advertised so that objections can be considered before registration is completed.

  1. Application: The representative applicant submits information about the goods, geographical area, origin-linked characteristics and producers.
  2. Examination: The GI Registry examines whether the application satisfies the statutory requirements and may seek clarification.
  3. Publication: An accepted application is advertised in the Geographical Indications Journal.
  4. Opposition: A person may oppose registration within 3 months of advertisement. The Registrar may permit an extension of up to 1 additional month.
  5. Registration: If no successful opposition prevents registration and the requirements are satisfied, the GI is entered in the register and a certificate is issued.

Under section 16, the registered GI is treated as registered from the date of application, even when its certificate is issued later. Consequently, the filing date, certificate date and renewal-expiry date must not be confused.

Registered proprietor and authorised user

The GI register is divided into 2 parts:

  • Part A: Contains particulars of registered geographical indications and their registered proprietors.
  • Part B: Contains particulars of registered authorised users.

The registered proprietor is the organisation or body entered as proprietor of the GI. An authorised user is a person registered to use the GI in relation to the specified goods. A person claiming to be a producer may apply for authorised-user registration by applying in writing to the Registrar with a statement, supporting documents establishing producer status and the prescribed fee.

Registration gives authorised users the statutory exclusive right to use the GI for the covered goods, subject to conditions and limitations in the register. It does not mean that only 1 producer can use the GI. Multiple authorised users may coexist.

Duration and renewal

Registration of a GI lasts for 10 years and may be renewed for further periods of 10 years. An authorised user's registration lasts for 10 years or until the underlying GI registration expires, whichever is earlier. Renewal requires an application to the Registrar by the registered proprietor or authorised user, as applicable, and payment of the prescribed fee.

Because the Act treats the application date as the registration date, an official certificate issued several years after filing may show an expiry date calculated from the earlier filing date.

What protection does registration provide?

Section 21 gives the registered proprietor and authorised users the right to seek relief for infringement. A person who is not an authorised user may infringe a registered GI by presenting goods in a manner that misleads buyers about their geographical origin or amounts to unfair competition, including passing off.

Passing off occurs when goods are represented in a way that misleads buyers into believing they have another producer's or recognised product's commercial identity. Section 20 prevents an infringement action based on an unregistered GI under the Act, but it preserves available passing-off remedies.

Why GI rights cannot be commercially licensed

Section 24 establishes an unusually important rule: rights in a registered GI cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged like an ordinary transferable commercial asset. The Act makes an exception for the rights of a deceased authorised user passing to a successor in title under the applicable law.

Therefore, a producer cannot simply sell a GI right to an unrelated factory or grant that factory a licence to manufacture goods outside the registered geographical conditions. The right to use a GI comes from satisfying the statutory producer and authorised-user requirements, not from purchasing permission from a commercial owner.

Prelims focus

  • Section 7 divides the GI register into Part A for GIs and Part B for authorised users.
  • Section 17 deals with applications for authorised-user registration.
  • Section 18 provides a 10-year GI registration period with renewal.
  • Section 21 concerns rights conferred by registration; section 22 concerns infringement.
  • Section 24 prohibits assignment and licensing of registered GI rights.
  • Trap: The registered proprietor is not necessarily the only producer entitled to use the GI.

[Sources: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 7, 11, 13–14, 16–18 and 20–24; Intellectual Property India, 'Geographical Indications: An Introduction', sections on registration, authorised users and protection; consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: GI Registration, Authorised Users and Legal Protection in India

body:
Why Gujarat's crafts are important GI examples

Gujarat has distinctive traditions of weaving, dyeing, printing, embroidery, painting, stonework and furniture making. Many depend on specialised techniques passed between generations of artisans. Their products illustrate how human skill can create the geographical connection required for a GI.

The examples below appear as registered Gujarat GIs in the GI Registry's state-wise list dated 31 December 2025. This is a dated register extract, not a claim that no additional Gujarat GIs were registered during 2026.

Recognise the product, place and craft

Registered GIPlace or regional associationDistinctive identity
Patan PatolaPatanIntricate double-ikat silk weaving
Rajkot PatolaRajkot regionA distinct Patola weaving tradition, commonly associated with single ikat
Jamnagari BandhaniJamnagarTraditional tie-and-dye textiles
Kutch BandhaniKachchhRegional tie-and-dye textiles
Kutch AjrakhKachchhTraditional patterned textile block printing
Kutch Rogan CraftKachchhDecorative fabric painting using prepared coloured paste
Kutch EmbroideryKachchhRegional needlework and embroidery traditions
Gujarat Suf EmbroideryGujaratTraditional decorative embroidery
Tangaliya ShawlSaurashtra regionDistinctive dotted designs created during weaving
Surat Zari CraftSuratDecorative work associated with metallic threads
Gharchola Craft of GujaratGujaratTraditional ceremonial textiles
Ahmedabad Sodagari Block PrintAhmedabadA regional hand-block-printing tradition
Pethapur Printing BlocksPethapurCraft of producing blocks used for textile printing
Sankheda FurnitureSankhedaDecorated wooden furniture with a traditional finish
Agates of CambayKhambhatCraft products made using agate stone
Mata ni PachedhiGujaratTraditional painted and printed ritual textiles
Bharuch Sujani WeavingBharuchTraditional decorative textile work

Other registered Gujarat handicraft indications in the same dated list include Kachchh Shawls, Pithora and Surat Sadeli Craft. These names should be learnt as distinct products rather than treated as alternative names for one craft.

Patan Patola and Rajkot Patola are not identical

Ikat is a weaving technique in which yarns are tied and dyed according to a design before the fabric is woven. In double ikat, both sets of yarns—the lengthwise warp and the crosswise weft—are resist-dyed to produce the pattern. In single ikat, only one of these yarn systems is patterned in that way.

Patan Patola is especially recognised for its complex double-ikat tradition. Rajkot Patola has its own registered identity and is commonly associated with the simpler single-ikat method. The two are separately registered GIs, so their names should not be used interchangeably merely because both belong to the wider Patola family.

Bandhani, Ajrakh and Rogan are different techniques

Bandhani is a tie-and-dye technique. Small portions of cloth are tightly tied before dyeing; when the ties are removed, the resisted areas produce patterns. Gujarat has separately registered Jamnagari Bandhani and Kutch Bandhani.

Ajrakh involves patterned textile printing and dyeing, including the skilled use of wooden blocks. It is not simply another name for Bandhani.

Rogan is decorative painting on fabric using a prepared coloured paste. In Kachchh's tradition, castor-oil-based material is associated with this technique. Its method differs from both tie-dyeing and block printing.

Pethapur Printing Blocks adds another distinction: the registered product concerns the specialised blocks used in printing. It should not be confused with a registration for every printed textile made using those blocks.

Why some Gujarat GI names appear more than once

The 31 December 2025 state-wise list contains separate entries for Sankheda Furniture (Logo), Agates of Cambay (Logo) and Kutch Embroidery (Logo), in addition to entries for the corresponding product names. A logo-related registration is not evidence that a completely new traditional product has been identified.

This matters when interpreting lists or counts of registered GIs: an entry for a product name and an additional logo entry may appear separately in official records.

Prelims focus

  • Patan Patola is associated with Patan and double-ikat weaving.
  • Rajkot Patola is a separate GI, commonly associated with single ikat.
  • Jamnagari Bandhani and Kutch Bandhani are separately registered indications.
  • Kutch Ajrakh is associated with textile printing; Kutch Rogan Craft with fabric painting.
  • Sankheda Furniture, Agates of Cambay and Surat Zari Craft are registered Gujarat handicraft GIs.
  • Trap: Patola, Bandhani, Ajrakh and Rogan are not interchangeable craft techniques.

[Sources: Geographical Indications Registry, 'State wise Registered GI of India', details of applications registered as on 31 December 2025, Gujarat entries; Gujarat Tourism, 'Patola', Patan section; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, 'Handicraft', sections 'Ajrakh', 'Bandhani' and 'Rogan'; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, chapter 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14; online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
